intro: This branch puts derivatives to work: estimating values, describing motion, finding the highest and lowest points of a graph, and solving real "best possible" problems.

VI.3.01.what: Writing the equation of the line that just touches a curve at a point, and of the line at right angles to it.

levels.a: Finds the slope of the touching line from the derivative at the point.
levels.b: Writes the line's equation using the point and the slope.
levels.c: Writes the equation of the perpendicular line (the normal line).
levels.d: Finds the points where the touching line is flat.

VI.3.02.what: Using the touching line as a quick estimate for a curve near a known point, like estimating the square root of 4.1.

levels.a: Explains why the tangent line stays close to the curve nearby.
levels.b: Uses the tangent line to approximate a hard-to-compute value.
levels.c: Decides whether the estimate is too high or too low from the curve's bend.
levels.d: Uses differentials (tiny changes) to estimate small errors.

VI.3.03.what: Using derivatives to describe moving objects: position, speed and acceleration.

levels.a: Finds velocity by differentiating position.
levels.b: Finds acceleration by differentiating velocity.
levels.c: Decides whether an object is speeding up or slowing down.
levels.d: Finds the total distance traveled, including trips back and forth.

VI.3.04.what: Reading a derivative as a real-world rate, such as dollars per item or people per year.

levels.a: Explains the meaning of a derivative at a point, including its units.
levels.b: Interprets marginal cost, the cost of making one more item.
levels.c: Interprets rates of population growth.
levels.d: Estimates a rate from real data in a table.

VI.3.05.what: Setting up problems where two quantities change together over time, like the radius and area of a spreading puddle.

levels.a: Draws a diagram and labels the changing quantities.
levels.b: Finds an equation linking the quantities.
levels.c: Differentiates that equation with respect to time.
levels.d: Plugs in the given numbers only at the end, after differentiating.

VI.3.06.what: Classic linked-rates problems, such as a sliding ladder or a filling cone-shaped tank.

levels.a: Solves the sliding ladder problem.
levels.b: Solves for how fast water rises in a filling cone.
levels.c: Solves for how fast a shadow grows as someone walks.
levels.d: Solves problems where an angle is changing, using trigonometry.

VI.3.07.what: Critical points are where a graph is flat or has a sharp point. They are the candidates for peaks and valleys.

levels.a: Finds points where the derivative equals zero.
levels.b: Finds points where the derivative does not exist.
levels.c: Finds all critical points of a function.
levels.d: Explains why not every critical point is a peak or a valley.

VI.3.08.what: Using the sign of the derivative to tell where a graph is rising and where it is falling.

levels.a: Links a positive derivative to rising and a negative one to falling.
levels.b: Makes a sign chart showing where the derivative is positive or negative.
levels.c: Writes the stretches of x where the function rises or falls.
levels.d: Reads rising and falling parts from a graph of the derivative.

VI.3.09.what: Deciding whether a critical point is a peak or valley by checking if the graph switches between rising and falling there.

levels.a: Checks whether the derivative changes sign at a point.
levels.b: Identifies a local peak where rising switches to falling.
levels.c: Identifies a local valley where falling switches to rising.
levels.d: Justifies the conclusion in clear sentences.

VI.3.10.what: Concavity describes the way a graph bends: cupped upward like a bowl or downward like a dome.

levels.a: Links the sign of the second derivative to the bend.
levels.b: Recognizes cupped-up and cupped-down shapes.
levels.c: Finds the stretches of x where the graph bends each way.
levels.d: Explains cupped-up as the slope steadily increasing.

VI.3.11.what: Inflection points are where a graph switches its bend, from bowl-shaped to dome-shaped or back.

levels.a: Identifies points where the bend changes direction.
levels.b: Explains why a zero second derivative alone does not guarantee a switch.
levels.c: Finds all inflection points of a function.
levels.d: Finds inflection points from a graph of the derivative.

VI.3.12.what: A quicker test for peaks and valleys: at a flat point, a bowl shape means a valley and a dome shape means a peak.

levels.a: Identifies a valley where the slope is zero and the graph bends up.
levels.b: Identifies a peak where the slope is zero and the graph bends down.
levels.c: Recognizes when the test gives no answer and another test is needed.
levels.d: Justifies conclusions from the test in words.

VI.3.13.what: Finding the very highest and lowest values a function reaches over a whole stretch, not just local peaks.

levels.a: States that an unbroken function on a closed stretch has a highest and lowest value.
levels.b: Lists the candidates: critical points and the two endpoints.
levels.c: Compares the candidates' values to pick the highest and lowest.
levels.d: Handles open stretches, where a highest or lowest value may not exist.

VI.3.14.what: The mean value theorem: on any smooth trip, at some moment your instant speed equals your average speed.

levels.a: Uses Rolle's theorem: if you end where you started, somewhere the slope is zero.
levels.b: States the mean value theorem in plain words.
levels.c: Finds the exact point where the instant rate equals the average rate.
levels.d: Uses it to prove a driver must have broken a speed limit.

VI.3.15.what: Drawing an accurate graph of a function by gathering all the clues calculus gives about its shape.

levels.a: Finds the allowed inputs and where the graph crosses the axes.
levels.b: Finds the lines the graph approaches (asymptotes).
levels.c: Makes charts of rising, falling and bending from the derivatives.
levels.d: Combines everything into a complete, labeled sketch.

VI.3.16.what: Reading a function, its derivative and its second derivative side by side to see how their shapes connect.

levels.a: Matches three graphs to the function and its two derivatives.
levels.b: Describes features of the function from its derivative's graph.
levels.c: Describes features of the function from its second derivative's graph.
levels.d: Justifies each claim with precise language.

VI.3.17.what: Turning a word problem about the biggest or smallest possible value into a single formula to work with.

levels.a: Identifies the quantity to make as large or small as possible.
levels.b: Writes the limiting condition, like a fixed amount of fencing, as an equation.
levels.c: Combines them into a formula in just one variable.
levels.d: States the sensible range of values the variable can take.

VI.3.18.what: Solving "best possible" problems, like the largest area a fence can enclose, using derivatives.

levels.a: Finds the critical points of the formula.
levels.b: Tests them to confirm which gives the best value.
levels.c: Answers the question actually asked, with units.
levels.d: Solves classic fence, open-box and soup-can problems from start to finish.

VI.3.19.what: L'Hôpital's rule: when a limit gives zero over zero, you can often compare the rates of top and bottom instead.

levels.a: Recognizes the forms where the rule applies: zero over zero and infinity over infinity.
levels.b: Applies the rule by differentiating top and bottom separately.
levels.c: Applies it repeatedly when the first try still gives zero over zero.
levels.d: Rewrites other tricky forms, like zero times infinity, so the rule applies.

VI.3.20.what: Newton's method: a way to hunt down solutions to hard equations by following tangent lines toward where a graph crosses zero.

levels.a: Explains how following a tangent line gives a better guess.
levels.b: Writes the formula that turns one guess into the next.
levels.c: Runs a few steps by hand or calculator to close in on a solution.
levels.d: Recognizes situations where the method fails or wanders off.

VI.3.21.what: Solving an equation by rewriting it as x equals something, then feeding each answer back in until it settles.

levels.a: Rearranges an equation into the form x equals a formula in x.
levels.b: Repeats the formula, plugging each answer back in.
levels.c: Draws cobweb and staircase diagrams to show the process.
levels.d: Decides when the process settles down and when it runs away.
